title: Odes of Solomon

stories.title: 📜 Odes of Solomon
summaryBullets: A collection of 42 early Christian hymns from the late 1st to early 2nd century, originally composed in Syriac or Greek by a Jewish Christian author with Essene-Johannine affinities.
They emphasize Messiah’s advent, living water, joyful thanksgiving, and believers’ mystical union with the Beloved.
Themes echo Johannine theology: Christ as the preexistent Word (Ode 31), the light of the nations, the door to salvation, and the beloved to whom believers respond.
The hymns display early Trinitarian imagery and baptismal motifs, including the Spirit as feminine and intimate union with God.
Though not included in the canon, they influenced early worship in Syriac contexts and reflect proto-orthodox Christology.
crossRefs: John 4:10-14: Jesus tells the woman at the well that whoever drinks the water he gives will never thirst again, because it becomes in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life, the image that runs through this collection harder than any other.

John 7:37-39: On the last day of the feast Jesus stands and calls anyone who is thirsty to come to him and drink, and John explains that he was speaking of the Spirit those who believed were to receive.

John 1:1-3: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made through him, the doctrine the thirty-first song in this collection sets out in verse.

Isaiah 7:14: The virgin shall conceive and bear a son and shall call his name Immanuel, the prophecy standing behind the nineteenth song, which describes the conception and the birth in its own images.

Genesis 3:16: To the woman God says he will greatly multiply her pain in childbearing, and in pain she will bring forth children, the sentence the nineteenth song sets aside when it says the birth came without pain and called for no midwife.
Luke 1:26-38: Gabriel tells Mary that the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the power of the Most High overshadow her, the annunciation the same song sets to music without naming her.

1 Peter 3:18-20: Christ, put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit, went and preached to the spirits in prison, which is exactly where the last song in this collection ends, with the dead running to him and being let go.

Revelation 19:1-6: A great multitude in heaven cries Hallelujah four times over the fall of Babylon and the reign of God, the only place the New Testament keeps the Hebrew word that closes every song in this collection.

translationNotes.note: A dialect of Aramaic, the literary and church language of Edessa in northern Mesopotamia, written in its own script. The complete text of this collection survives only in Syriac. The Syriac Bible is called the Peshitta, meaning the simple or plain version. Aramaic is the language Jesus speaks in the Gospels, as at Mark 5:41 and Mark 15:34, where the Greek stops to spell out his words letter by letter and then translate them.

Two words: praise, in the plural imperative, and Yah, the short form of the divine name. No translator ever rendered it; it was carried across untranslated into Greek, Latin, Syriac and English alike. Every song in this collection ends with it. Psalm 150 opens and closes with it, and Revelation 19:1-6 is the only place it stands in the New Testament.

A sung poem. Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 both put the word third in a list, telling believers to speak to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. These forty-two pieces are the earliest collection of Christian hymns that survives anywhere.

Nothing in these songs mentions Solomon, his reign or his temple. The name comes from the superscriptions the manuscripts carry and from the ancient book lists. Songs gravitate to his name because 1 Kings 4:32 says he spoke three thousand proverbs and his songs were a thousand and five. This collection is constantly confused with the Psalms of Solomon, which is a different book: eighteen Jewish psalms written in Hebrew in the first century BC.

Hebrew calls running water living water, as against standing water in a cistern. Leviticus 14:5 requires it for cleansing, poured over an earthen vessel. Jeremiah 2:13 has God charge Israel with two evils, forsaking the fountain of living waters and hewing out cracked cisterns that hold none. John 4:10-14 takes the phrase over, and these songs run it through image after image.

Not a king's diadem. A stephanos is the woven wreath handed to a victor at the games or set on a guest at a feast, and that is the word the New Testament uses for the believer's reward: 1 Corinthians 9:25 for an imperishable wreath, James 1:12 for the crown of life, Revelation 2:10 for the crown given to the one faithful to the point of death. In these songs the crown on the singer's head is alive and puts out branches.

The nineteenth song describes a cup of milk offered and drunk, and then names its parts: the Son is the cup, the Father is the one who was milked, and the Holy Spirit is she who milked him. The song goes on to the virgin conceiving, bearing without pain, and calling for no midwife. Lactantius quotes this song as Solomon's in the Divine Institutes 4.12.3, written about AD 304 to 311, which is the earliest quotation of the collection anywhere.

In Syriac, as in Hebrew, the word for spirit is grammatically feminine, and early Syriac writers used feminine verbs and pronouns with it as a matter of grammar. Genesis 1:2 has the ruach of God hovering over the face of the waters. Greek pneuma is neuter and Latin spiritus is masculine, so the gender of the word shifts with the language it is written in.

A lyre, carried in the arms and plucked, not the tall floor harp a modern reader pictures. It is the instrument David played to quiet Saul, and the instrument the exiles hang on the willows at Psalm 137:2 when their captors ask them for a song of Zion. These songs use it for the singer himself, strung and played by the Spirit.

The title these songs use most often for the Messiah. Matthew 3:17 has the voice at the baptism say, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Ephesians 1:6 says believers are accepted in the Beloved. Isaiah 5:1 opens a song about the vineyard of my beloved, which is the Old Testament's way of using it.

A mark of ownership pressed into wax or clay with a signet, used on a document, a jar, a slave or a soldier. These songs speak of the singer being sealed, which is how early Christian writing talks about baptism. 2 Corinthians 1:22 says God sealed us and gave the Spirit as a down payment, Ephesians 1:13 has believers sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, and Revelation 7:3 has the servants of God sealed on their foreheads.

A Coptic work the British Museum acquired in 1785, and for a long time the only witness to any of this collection. It quotes five of these songs in full or in part, and one of them survives nowhere else at all. Before the Syriac manuscripts turned up, this book and a single Latin quotation were the whole of what anyone had.

In 1909 J. Rendel Harris identified a Syriac manuscript acquired from the neighbourhood of the Tigris, now John Rylands Library Cod. Syr. 9, which starts partway through the third song, runs to the end of the collection, and then carries straight on into the Psalms of Solomon. In 1912 F. C. Burkitt identified a second Syriac witness in the British Museum, a tenth-century codex from the Syrian monastery in the Nitrian Desert that had been sitting in England since 1843.

A Greek copy of the eleventh song, written in the third century and published by Michel Testuz in 1959. It carries seven lines the Syriac does not have. That one leaf is the proof the collection existed in Greek, and it sets the outside limit on how late these songs can possibly be.

Spoken against. Eusebius of Caesarea uses the word in the Ecclesiastical History 3.25 for books read in some churches and disputed in others, as distinct from the accepted books and from the ones rejected outright. The Stichometry of Nicephorus counts this collection and the Psalms of Solomon as a single entry of 2,100 lines and files them among the antilegomena, which is part of why the two books keep getting confused.

translationNotes.term: The descent in the last song
translationNotes.note: The forty-second and last song ends with the Messiah going down to the place of the dead, the dead running to him and calling out, and his opening the door and letting them go. Psalm 16:10 says God will not abandon his soul to Sheol or let his holy one see corruption, and Acts 2:27 quotes that verse at Pentecost. 1 Peter 3:18-20 has him preach to the spirits in prison.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Odes of Solomon are a joyful, mystical hymn anthology celebrating union with the Messiah, rich in Johannine and early Christian imagery.

intro:
The Odes of Solomon are forty-two songs, and they are the earliest collection of Christian hymns that survives. They are transmitted under Solomon's name, as the Psalms of Solomon are, and the two books are constantly confused with each other. They are not the same book. The Psalms of Solomon are eighteen Jewish psalms written in Hebrew in the first century BC about the fall of Jerusalem to Pompey; the Odes are Christian hymns, and their subject is the Messiah who has come. The confusion has a cause: ancient lists count the two works as one entry, and the Syriac manuscript that first brought the Odes back to light carries both, the Odes first and the Psalms of Solomon after them.

The odes are first-person songs of praise and thanksgiving. Recurring images run through them: living water and the spring that never fails, the crown set on the singer's head, the harp of the Spirit, the Beloved and the union of the believer with Him, milk and the cup, the open door, light against darkness, and the Word that goes out from the Most High. Several odes speak in the voice of the Messiah rather than about Him, among them 8, 10, 17, 22, 28, 31, and 42, which ends with the descent to the place of the dead and the release of those who called on Him. Ode 19 speaks of the Son, the Spirit, and the virgin conception and birth. Ode 11 describes the singer led into paradise. No author is named anywhere in the collection.

The manuscript history is a recovery story. Before the modern discoveries the Odes were known only from a Latin quotation and from lists of apocryphal books. Lactantius quotes the nineteenth ode as Solomon's in the Divine Institutes 4.12.3, written about AD 304 to 311. The Coptic Pistis Sophia, which the British Museum acquired in 1785, quotes five odes in full or in part, Ode 1, Ode 5, Ode 6, Ode 22, and Ode 25; Ode 1 survives nowhere else. In 1909 J. Rendel Harris identified a Syriac manuscript acquired from the neighborhood of the Tigris, now John Rylands Library Cod. Syr. 9, which begins partway through Ode 3 and runs to the end of Ode 42 before continuing into the Psalms of Solomon; Ode 2 is lost entirely and Ode 1 is missing from it. In 1912 F. C. Burkitt identified a second Syriac witness in the British Museum, Add. 14538, a tenth-century codex from the Syrian Monastery in the Nitrian Desert that had been in England since 1843 and that carries Ode 17:7 through Ode 42:20. A Greek copy of Ode 11 turned up among the Bodmer papyri, Papyrus Bodmer XI, written in the third century and published by Michel Testuz in 1959; it contains seven lines the Syriac does not have.

The language of composition is not settled. The complete text exists only in Syriac, and one ode exists in Greek, close enough to the Syriac that either could stand behind the other. The dating proposals spread across two centuries and are argued from the text itself, since the external limits are wide: Papyrus Bodmer XI puts the collection in Greek in the third century, and Lactantius puts Ode 19 in Latin hands by about AD 310. Adolf von Harnack, with Johannes Flemming in 1910, argued that a Jewish hymnbook underlies the collection and that a Christian hand worked it over. Brian McNeil argued for a date around AD 100, Luise Abramowski for the second half of the second century, and Han Drijvers for the third. The Stichometry of Nicephorus, from the ninth century, lists the Psalms and Odes of Solomon together at 2,100 lines among the antilegomena, the disputed books. No communion receives the Odes of Solomon as canonical.
